obtained.how: ASLO's own free PDF of the article (aslo.org/lo/toc/vol_35/issue_4/0795.pdf), as captured by the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine on 22 Jun 2006 and openly downloadable; Wiley, today's host, refuses scripts (403). 14 pages, OCR text layer; Table 3 read in the raw text

bibliography.checked_against: the article's first page (p. 795) and Crossref
bibliography.note: Michael L. Pace, George B. McManus & Stuart E. G. Findlay, Limnol. Oceanogr. 35(4): 795–808 (1990), title as cited. Printed page = PDF page + 794

claims.claim: in Upton Lake D. galeata "consumed most of the bacterial production" except in winter and autumn
claims.location: p. 795 (PDF p. 1), abstract; p. 801 (PDF p. 7), Results; p. 805 (PDF p. 11), Discussion
claims.quote: At other times, Daphnia galeata consumed most of the bacterial production.
claims.conditions: Upton Lake, Dutchess County, New York: 18 ha, eutrophic, ice ~3 months, anoxic or < 1 mg O₂/L bottom water; five paired day–night experiments in 1988 (March under ice, April, July, September, October) on 2-m water; grazing measured with E. coli minicells (fluorescent or radiolabelled), growth by thymidine incorporation
claims.note: the abstract's preceding sentence gives the exception: 'Flagellates were the primary consumers of bacteria in winter and fall'. In the body the fall shift is clearest in October (flagellate feeding above macrozooplankton feeding; Daphnia scarce, Dinobryon divergens abundant); in July 'the primary fate of bacterial production' was 'direct ingestion by Daphnia' (p. 801). The paper's '(… ; abstract only)' tag can go: the full text bears it out

claims.claim: ciliates and rotifers "were never important bacterial grazers" (Upton Lake)
claims.location: p. 795 (PDF p. 1), abstract; p. 799 (PDF p. 5), Methods; p. 803 (PDF p. 9), Results
claims.quote: Ciliates and rotifers were never important bacterial grazers.
claims.conditions: the 35–200-µm fraction, dominated by Polyarthra and Keratella, took up little more radioactivity than killed controls, so the authors report only macrozooplankton (p. 799); ciliate grazing (1.2–96 × 10⁴ bacteria L⁻¹ h⁻¹) was typically < 10 % of flagellate grazing (p. 803)
claims.note: worth carrying into the text: the rotifers were mainly Polyarthra and Keratella and were judged 'not feeding on bacteria at significant rates' by a radiotracer test against killed controls (p. 799); the tracer minicells are small (0.6–0.7 µm), DNA-free cells of a mutant E. coli (p. 797)

claims.location: p. 795 (PDF p. 1), abstract; p. 804 (PDF p. 10), Table 3; p. 803 (PDF p. 9)
claims.quote: turnover times calculated from either growth or grazing rates ranged from 1.5 to 16 d
claims.conditions: Table 3 (raw text): spring–fall turnover 6.1–16.3 d from growth, 1.5–12.7 d from grazing, 2.5–9.1 d from total mortality; under ice on 3 March 55.9 d (growth) and 90.9 d (grazing) — 'Exceptionally slow turnover times of 50-100 d were observed under the ice in March'
claims.note: the 1.5–16 d range is the open-water season only; the abstract leaves out the winter values. BACT_LOSS 0.15/d (≈ 6.7 d at 20 °C, × MICROBE.Q10 in the cold) sits inside it. The authors also compiled 29 thymidine-based cases from the literature: mean turnover 4.5 d, median 3.7, range 0.5–14 (p. 805)

notes: Every claim checks; drop the 'abstract only' tag in §3.3.8. Useful elsewhere in §3.3.8: Pace et al. cite Cole et al. 1988 as 'bacterial production is ~30% of primary production on an areal basis' (p. 795), whereas §3.3.8 gives Cole et al.'s average as about 20 % — the two may be volumetric vs areal; worth checking against Cole et al. 1988 itself. Pace et al. also report Sanders et al. 1989's Lake Oglethorpe result as heterotrophic and mixotrophic flagellates taking 68–90 % of bacterial ingestion (p. 805), while §3.3.8 gives 49–81 % for heterotrophic nanoflagellates (Sanders et al., abstract only) — not a contradiction if the 49–81 % excludes mixotrophs, but the reader of that entry should check. Seasonal community loss rates of minicells were 0.1–0.2 d⁻¹, 0.3–0.4 d⁻¹ in July (p. 803).
